messages.content: I want to design a restartable device-driver isolation boundary that contains DMA faults without invalidating hard-real-time guarantees for unaffected devices. What exactly has to hold?

The boundary has two simultaneous obligations. It must contain arbitrary driver memory writes, DMA, and interrupt storms across driver crashes and restarts. At the same time, unaffected devices must retain verified 1 ms service deadlines during driver faults and concurrent recovery. Containment alone is not enough if handling a fault or restarting a driver makes another device miss that deadline.
Why call out arbitrary driver memory writes separately from DMA?

They are distinct sources of effects that the boundary must contain. Arbitrary driver memory writes cover what faulty driver code might write. DMA must also be covered because device-initiated memory activity cannot be treated as though it were merely an ordinary write by the driver. The goal requires containment of both; it does not say that constraining one automatically constrains the other.
And interrupt storms are part of the same requirement?

Yes. An interrupt storm is explicitly in scope alongside driver memory writes and DMA. The boundary must contain its effects, including when a driver crashes or restarts. In particular, containing memory effects would not by itself establish that unaffected devices can still receive service within their verified 1 ms deadlines.
Does the boundary only need to work while the driver is running normally?

No. The requirement expressly extends across driver crashes and restarts. The design cannot rely on normal driver operation as the condition under which containment holds. Fault handling and recovery are part of the situation the boundary has to accommodate.
So is restarting the driver itself the measure of success?

Restartability is necessary to the goal, but it is not the whole measure. The boundary must continue to contain arbitrary driver memory writes, DMA, and interrupt storms across crashes and restarts. It must also preserve the verified 1 ms service deadlines of unaffected devices while faults occur and recovery runs concurrently.
What does “unaffected devices” mean for the timing requirement?

It identifies the devices whose service guarantees must not be invalidated by another driver's fault or recovery. The stated 1 ms deadline applies to those unaffected devices. The goal does not specify an equivalent service deadline for the faulting driver or say how quickly its recovery must finish.
Could the unaffected devices pause during recovery and make up the time afterward?

Not if that pause causes them to miss a verified 1 ms service deadline. The requirement includes concurrent recovery, so a later return to normal service would not, by itself, satisfy it. The deadline has to remain valid while recovery is taking place.
Does “verified” just mean that 1 ms seems achievable in ordinary operation?

No. A hard-real-time service deadline is not an average or an expectation about ordinary operation. The goal is to retain a verified 1 ms deadline for unaffected devices during driver faults and concurrent recovery. The node states that required assurance, not that a verification has already been completed or that a particular verification method has been chosen.
Suppose the memory effects are contained, but dealing with an interrupt storm delays another device's service. Would that satisfy the goal?

No. It would address only part of the goal. Interrupt storms must be contained too, and the unaffected device must still retain its verified 1 ms service deadline. The safety aspect of isolation and the timing guarantee have to hold together.
Is it fair to say the isolation boundary must remain meaningful during the transition from a crashed driver to a restarted one?

Yes. “Across driver crashes and restarts” includes that transition; containment cannot depend on assuming that recovery is already complete. That statement does not prescribe a particular restart procedure. It describes the continuity the boundary must provide.
Would containing DMA only after the new driver starts be sufficient?

No. DMA containment is required across the crash and restart, not only after a restarted driver is operating. The goal leaves the means of doing that open, but it does not leave a gap in the containment requirement during recovery.
I want to avoid quietly turning this into a general claim that every device meets a 1 ms deadline. Is that distinction important?

Yes. The stated deadline is for unaffected devices during driver faults and concurrent recovery. It should not be broadened into a claim about every device in every state, nor narrowed to a claim that only holds when no fault or recovery is underway.
What can we say about the design without choosing its mechanisms yet?

We can state the obligations the mechanisms must meet: contain arbitrary driver memory writes, DMA, and interrupt storms; maintain that containment through driver crashes and restarts; and preserve verified 1 ms service deadlines for unaffected devices during faults and concurrent recovery. Those obligations define what a proposed isolation boundary would need to demonstrate without selecting an implementation.
So the timing condition is not merely an extra performance preference?

Correct. It is a hard-real-time requirement of the goal. A boundary that contains the fault but invalidates the verified 1 ms service deadline for an unaffected device would not meet the stated objective. Fault containment and continued deadline assurance are both essential.
And if recovery is happening at the same time as unaffected devices need service, that concurrency is explicitly in scope?

It is. The requirement says unaffected devices retain their verified 1 ms service deadlines during driver faults and concurrent recovery. Recovery therefore cannot be treated as a separate interval during which those deadlines are set aside.
What architecture would you propose for the restartable driver boundary?

I would propose per-driver MMU and IOMMU domains, remapped maskable interrupts, restarts that quiesce or reset DMA, and budgeted recovery kept separate from reserved real-time cores. These are proposed mechanisms for containing driver memory writes, DMA, and interrupt storms while protecting the verified 1 ms service deadlines of unaffected devices. The proposal itself is not yet a verification of those deadlines.
Why specify both an MMU domain and an IOMMU domain for each driver?

They address different paths to memory. A per-driver MMU domain is the proposed boundary for memory accesses made by driver code. A per-driver IOMMU domain is the proposed boundary for DMA. Calling for both avoids assuming that isolation of the driver's own writes also contains device-initiated writes.
Does “per-driver” matter here, or would a single domain for all drivers express the same idea?

Per-driver separation is part of the proposal. The intent is to give a driver its own isolation boundary rather than treating all drivers as one unit for these memory-access controls. The proposal does not specify the contents of each domain or the detailed mapping policy.
How do remapped maskable interrupts fit with the memory domains?

They address a different part of containment. MMU and IOMMU domains concern memory access; remapping and maskability provide a proposed way to control interrupt delivery when a driver or its device produces an interrupt storm. That control matters because a storm could threaten service time for unaffected devices even if memory accesses remain isolated.
Are you saying an interrupt storm is harmless as soon as interrupts can be masked?

No. Maskability is a proposed control, not a timing proof. Its use, together with interrupt remapping, would have to preserve service for unaffected devices, including their verified 1 ms deadlines. The proposal does not claim that merely having a maskable interrupt makes every possible storm harmless.
What does “DMA-quiesce/reset restarts” mean in this proposal?

It means that restarting a driver is not treated as only restarting its code. The proposed restart approach also quiesces or resets DMA activity associated with the faulting driver, so that DMA containment remains relevant through the crash and restart. The wording does not prescribe a particular device-specific reset procedure or claim that a restart has already been demonstrated.
Why can't the driver simply be restarted while DMA continues?

The goal requires DMA faults to be contained across crashes and restarts. Simply restarting driver code would not, by itself, address DMA that may still be active. Quiescing or resetting DMA is therefore an explicit part of the proposed restart boundary. Whether a particular implementation achieves the required containment would still need to be established.
Where does budgeted recovery come in?

Recovery itself can consume processing time, so the proposal makes it budgeted rather than treating it as unbounded work. It also keeps that recovery separate from reserved real-time cores. Those choices are aimed at allowing recovery to proceed concurrently without taking away the capacity reserved for the unaffected devices' real-time service.
Is there a recovery budget value in the proposal?

No numerical recovery budget is specified. “Budgeted recovery” is a proposed constraint on recovery work, not a stated budget size or a deadline for completing the restart. The explicit numerical timing requirement remains the verified 1 ms service deadline for unaffected devices.
Does keeping recovery off the reserved real-time cores prove the 1 ms deadline on its own?

No. Separating budgeted recovery from those cores is one part of the proposal, but it does not by itself establish the full timing guarantee. Driver faults, DMA activity, and interrupt storms also have to be contained in a way that leaves the unaffected devices' verified 1 ms service deadlines intact during concurrent recovery.
Should I understand “reserved real-time cores” as a specific number of cores?

No count is given. The proposal distinguishes cores reserved for real-time work from the resources used for budgeted recovery, but it does not specify how many cores are reserved or lay out a particular processor configuration.
I want the isolation boundary to survive a crash, not just exist during ordinary driver execution. Does the proposal address that distinction?

That is the reason the restart and recovery elements are included alongside the domains and interrupts. The proposed boundary has to remain effective when a driver crashes and while it is being restarted: memory writes and DMA still need containment, an interrupt storm still needs control, and recovery must not invalidate the unaffected devices' verified 1 ms deadlines. Naming these mechanisms does not yet establish that a specific implementation has achieved all of that.
Could I describe this as four coordinated controls rather than one isolation switch?

Yes. Per-driver MMU/IOMMU domains address driver and DMA memory access; remapped maskable interrupts address interrupt delivery; DMA-quiesce/reset restarts address the transition through failure and restart; and budgeted recovery separate from reserved real-time cores addresses recovery's use of execution time. They are coordinated parts of one proposed boundary, not interchangeable substitutes.
Would the proposal allow us to ignore timing once a fault has been isolated to its own domain?

No. Keeping a fault within a domain addresses only part of the requirement. Unaffected devices must retain their verified 1 ms service deadlines during the fault and concurrent recovery. The interrupt and recovery provisions in the proposal speak directly to that timing concern, while the full guarantee would still require verification.
What should we avoid asserting when presenting this as a proposal?

We should not present the 1 ms deadline as already verified under this architecture, claim that recovery completes within a particular time, or assume that one mechanism alone covers every fault channel. The proposal identifies per-driver MMU/IOMMU domains, remapped maskable interrupts, DMA-quiesce/reset restarts, and budgeted recovery away from reserved real-time cores as the approach to evaluate against the containment and timing requirements.
How can driver DMA and interrupts be revoked during restart without consuming unaffected devices’ reserved 1 ms service budgets?

The proposed approach is to make revocation part of the faulting driver's isolation and budgeted recovery path, rather than work charged to the service reserved for unaffected devices. Its per-driver IOMMU domain provides a boundary for DMA, remapped maskable interrupts provide a way to control interrupt delivery, and DMA quiescence or reset is part of restart. Recovery is proposed to run separately from reserved real-time cores. Whether that arrangement actually preserves the unaffected devices’ verified 1 ms service deadlines must still be established, including during revocation itself.
Does that mean we can wait until the restarted driver is running before revoking its DMA access?

No. The question is specifically about revocation during restart, when the crashed driver cannot be assumed to control its device. A restart approach must account for DMA activity through that interval, not merely restore a driver and address access afterward. The proposal names per-driver IOMMU domains and DMA quiescence or reset, but does not specify a detailed revocation sequence.
How do interrupts differ from DMA in this question?

DMA and interrupts pose different problems for the unaffected devices. DMA concerns device-initiated memory access; interrupt delivery can consume attention and disrupt timely service, particularly during a storm. The proposal therefore has separate controls: the IOMMU domain and DMA-quiesce/reset restart for DMA, and remapped maskable interrupts for interrupt delivery. Both controls have to remain effective during fault handling and restart.
If the faulting driver's interrupts are maskable, can we just count that as meeting the timing requirement?

Not on its own. Maskability offers a means of revocation, but the requirement is about what happens while interrupts are being controlled and recovery proceeds. The unaffected devices must still retain their verified 1 ms service deadlines. That requires accounting for the effects of the fault and the work of handling it, rather than inferring a deadline guarantee from the existence of a mask.
What does it mean not to consume an unaffected device's reserved service budget?

It means fault handling for one driver must not take the execution capacity reserved to service an unaffected device when that capacity is needed to maintain its 1 ms deadline. Budgeted recovery separate from reserved real-time cores is the proposed way to separate that work. The 1 ms figure is the unaffected device's service deadline; no numerical size for a recovery budget is specified.
Would putting the recovery work on different cores settle the issue?

It addresses where recovery execution runs, but it does not by itself settle the issue. DMA and interrupts can have effects beyond the recovery work's use of a core. To meet the goal, those effects and the act of revoking them must also be contained without invalidating the unaffected devices’ verified 1 ms service deadlines.
So the revocation operation itself is within the timing question, not just what happens afterward?

Exactly. A deadline that holds only after revocation finishes would not answer the question. The unaffected devices need their verified 1 ms service deadlines during the driver fault and concurrent recovery, which includes the period in which DMA and interrupts are being brought under control.
Could the design simply stop servicing unaffected devices briefly to make revocation faster?

Only if their verified 1 ms service deadlines remain intact; a brief interruption is not automatically harmless in a hard-real-time setting. The proposal's separation of budgeted recovery from reserved real-time cores is meant to avoid using those devices’ reserved service as the source of recovery time.
Is the idea to prevent any recovery activity from occurring while unaffected devices operate?

No. Concurrent recovery is explicitly in scope. The issue is how to bound and isolate recovery's demands, while revoking the faulting driver's DMA and interrupts, so that unaffected devices keep their verified 1 ms service deadlines. The proposal does not require recovery to wait until those devices are idle.
What if recovery work stays within its own budget, but the faulting device continues generating interrupts?

Then the recovery budget alone has not addressed the interrupt side of containment. Remapped maskable interrupts are proposed precisely because interrupt delivery needs its own control. The timing case must cover the faulting device's interrupts during restart as well as the processing time spent on recovery.
Likewise, would isolating the driver's ordinary memory writes be enough for DMA revocation?

No. Driver memory writes and device DMA are distinct paths. The per-driver MMU domain addresses the former in the proposal; the per-driver IOMMU domain and DMA-quiesce/reset restart address the latter. Revoking the driver's ability to write memory does not, by itself, demonstrate that device DMA is contained during restart.
Can we describe a required outcome for DMA revocation without choosing a device-specific procedure?

Yes. The required outcome is that DMA associated with the faulting driver remains contained across its crash and restart, including while it is being quiesced or reset, without defeating the unaffected devices’ verified 1 ms service deadlines. The current proposal does not choose a device-specific quiesce or reset procedure, so it should not be presented as though one has already been shown to work.
What would we need to keep in view when evaluating this approach?

Keep the fault interval and the restart interval in view, not just steady operation. For each, the questions are whether driver writes and DMA remain contained, whether interrupt storms can be controlled, and whether the work and effects of revocation and recovery leave unaffected devices able to meet their verified 1 ms service deadlines. Those are criteria for evaluating the proposal, not results already obtained.
Is there a stated time limit for completing DMA quiescence, interrupt revocation, or the whole restart?

No such completion time is specified. The explicit numerical requirement is that unaffected devices retain verified 1 ms service deadlines during faults and concurrent recovery. Revocation and restart must be compatible with that requirement, but the node does not assign them their own numerical deadline.
Could I say the desired separation is both spatial and temporal?

That is a useful conceptual description. Per-driver MMU/IOMMU domains concern memory-access separation; remapped maskable interrupts concern control over interrupt delivery; and budgeted recovery away from reserved real-time cores concerns the use of execution time. The important qualification is that this separation is proposed as a way to protect the unaffected devices’ 1 ms deadlines, not a claim that those deadlines have already been verified under faults and concurrent restart.
Then how should the central question be phrased when reviewing a candidate design?

Ask whether it can revoke or contain the faulting driver's DMA and interrupt effects throughout restart, while performing the necessary recovery within its own budget and without taking service reserved for unaffected devices. Then ask whether the unaffected devices’ verified 1 ms deadlines still hold during the fault and the concurrent revocation and recovery—not merely once restart is complete.

Here's a hypothesis for the revocation problem: recovery-core isolation, interrupt quotas, and IOMMU drain-before-reuse yield zero unaffected 1 ms misses during DMA floods and interrupt storms. How should we read that?

As a hypothesis about the combined effect of three controls, not as an observed result. Recovery-core isolation is intended to keep recovery work from consuming execution capacity reserved for unaffected devices. Interrupt quotas are intended to bound the service demanded by a storm. IOMMU drain-before-reuse is intended to account for outstanding DMA before IOMMU-controlled resources are reused. The predicted outcome is zero missed 1 ms service deadlines for unaffected devices during DMA floods and interrupt storms.
Does “zero unaffected 1 ms misses” mean the devices merely continue to function?

It is more specific than continued function. It predicts that unaffected devices have no misses of their 1 ms service deadlines under the stated DMA-flood and interrupt-storm conditions. A device could continue functioning and still miss a hard-real-time deadline, so those are not equivalent claims.
And we're not saying that outcome has already been measured?

Correct. The node states a hypothesis. It gives neither measurements nor a completed verification, so the zero-miss outcome should be presented as what these controls are expected to yield, not what has already been demonstrated.
How does recovery-core isolation relate to the earlier concern about taking time away from unaffected devices?

It targets the execution-time side of that concern. The idea is to isolate recovery activity from the cores reserved for real-time service, rather than let restart work consume the capacity on which unaffected devices depend. The hypothesis still has to account for DMA and interrupt effects; isolating recovery execution alone would not establish zero 1 ms misses.
Does the hypothesis assign a particular core count or recovery budget?

No. It names recovery-core isolation but specifies no number of cores, no numerical recovery budget, and no recovery-completion time. The stated numerical timing target is zero misses of unaffected devices’ 1 ms service deadlines during DMA floods and interrupt storms.
What role do interrupt quotas play if interrupts are already remapped and maskable in the proposal?

The quota adds the idea of bounding how much interrupt activity can demand while a storm is occurring. Remapping and maskability describe proposed control over interrupt delivery; a quota addresses the amount of interrupt-related work permitted. The hypothesis does not give a quota value, an accounting rule, or a particular enforcement mechanism.
Should I treat a quota as proof that a storm cannot disturb an unaffected device?

No. An interrupt quota is one element of the hypothesis. The claimed zero-miss outcome concerns the controls operating together during interrupt storms and DMA floods. A quota's existence alone is not evidence that unaffected devices meet every 1 ms service deadline.
I want to be precise about “IOMMU drain-before-reuse.” Is it simply another name for restarting the driver?

No. It identifies a DMA-related condition on reuse: outstanding activity governed by the IOMMU must be accounted for before the relevant protected resources are reused. Restarting driver code is a different matter. The hypothesis names drain-before-reuse without specifying a device-specific drain procedure or claiming that the drain has already been verified.
Why does the “before reuse” part matter to the hypothesis?

It makes the ordering explicit. The hypothesis does not assume that changing the driver's state immediately eliminates outstanding DMA effects. Drain-before-reuse is meant to avoid treating a resource as available for reuse while earlier DMA activity is still relevant to its isolation. That is a proposed contribution to the zero-miss outcome, not an established result by itself.
Are the DMA floods and interrupt storms separate conditions, or is this only about one at a time?

The hypothesis names both DMA floods and interrupt storms as conditions under which it predicts zero unaffected 1 ms misses. It does not specify a test matrix or say whether they occur separately or simultaneously. We should preserve both named conditions without adding a more detailed scenario.
Does “zero misses” allow a small number of late services as long as the average stays below 1 ms?

No. Zero misses is an absolute prediction about the specified 1 ms deadline, not an average-latency target or a tolerance for occasional late service. Its strength is also why it should be kept clearly labeled as a hypothesis until established.
Is the outcome about the faulting driver as well?
No. It is specifically about unaffected devices. The hypothesis does not set a 1 ms service deadline for the faulting driver, nor does it state how long its restart may take.
Could I reduce the hypothesis to “recovery is isolated, therefore there are no misses”?

That would leave out two explicitly named elements. The hypothesis combines recovery-core isolation, interrupt quotas, and IOMMU drain-before-reuse. It predicts zero unaffected 1 ms misses during DMA floods and interrupt storms from that combination, not from recovery-core isolation alone.
How does it answer the question about revoking DMA and interrupts during restart?

It offers a candidate explanation for how revocation and recovery might avoid consuming the unaffected devices’ reserved service: keep recovery execution isolated, bound interrupt demands with quotas, and drain IOMMU-governed DMA before reuse. Its prediction is that unaffected devices then suffer zero 1 ms misses during DMA floods and interrupt storms. It does not yet establish that the proposed controls achieve this in an implementation.
Should we say the IOMMU drain has a specific maximum duration?
No duration is specified. The hypothesis names drain-before-reuse as a condition; it does not provide a drain-time bound. Any claim about a maximum duration would add information not present here.
What if a design has all three named controls, but an unaffected device misses one 1 ms deadline during an interrupt storm?

That observation would not match the hypothesis's predicted zero-miss outcome for that condition. The distinction is between having the named controls and actually achieving the stated result. The hypothesis should not be treated as satisfied merely because the controls are present.
Can we claim these three controls solve every arbitrary driver fault?

Not from this hypothesis. It makes a particular prediction about unaffected devices’ 1 ms deadline misses during DMA floods and interrupt storms. The broader isolation goal also includes arbitrary driver memory writes and behavior across crashes and restarts, but this hypothesis should not be enlarged into an established solution for every fault.
Then the careful wording is that these controls are expected to yield zero deadline misses for unaffected devices under the named conditions?

Yes. “Recovery-core isolation, interrupt quotas, and IOMMU drain-before-reuse are hypothesized to yield zero unaffected-device 1 ms service-deadline misses during DMA floods and interrupt storms” preserves both the predicted outcome and its unverified status.
How should we evaluate the hypothesis about recovery-core isolation, interrupt quotas, and IOMMU drain-before-reuse?

Run 10,000 FaultBench-1 restart trials with rogue writes, stale DMA, and 100-kHz interrupts. Measure IOMMU drains and unaffected-device deadline misses. That activity is meant to evaluate the hypothesis that the controls yield zero unaffected-device 1 ms misses during DMA floods and interrupt storms; it is not a report that the trials have already been run.
Can you spell out the trial count without assuming a split among the faults?

The stated activity is 10,000 FaultBench-1 restart trials in total. It names rogue writes, stale DMA, and 100-kHz interrupts as fault conditions, but does not specify how the trials are divided among them or whether those conditions are applied together in any particular trial.
What should I take “restart trials” to mean here?

They are trials centered on a driver restart under the named fault conditions. That matters because the isolation boundary must remain effective across crashes and restarts, rather than only during ordinary driver operation. The activity does not specify a detailed restart sequence or a criterion for how quickly restart must complete.
Why include rogue writes when the hypothesis focuses on DMA floods and interrupt storms?

Rogue writes exercise the driver-memory-write part of the broader containment goal while the restart trials are run. Stale DMA addresses the DMA side, and 100-kHz interrupts address interrupt pressure. Including rogue writes does not change the hypothesis into a claim that every form of arbitrary write has already been contained.
What is the significance of calling the DMA stale?

It directs attention to DMA that may still be relevant when driver state changes through restart. That makes the proposed drain-before-reuse condition worth evaluating. The activity does not specify how stale DMA is generated, how long it persists, or a particular device behavior.
Is the interrupt condition a vague description of a storm, or does it have a stated rate?
It has a stated rate: 100-kHz interrupts. That is 100,000 interrupts per second. The activity does not add a duration, an interrupt source configuration, or a separate rate for each trial.
What exactly are we supposed to measure?

Two things are explicitly named: IOMMU drains and deadline misses for unaffected devices. Measuring the drains bears on the drain-before-reuse part of the hypothesis; measuring unaffected-device deadline misses bears on its predicted timing outcome. No measurement procedure or list of additional metrics is specified.
Could we replace deadline misses with average service latency?

Not as a substitute for the stated measurement. The hypothesis predicts zero misses of unaffected devices’ 1 ms service deadlines. An average could conceal a late service, so the activity specifically calls for measuring deadline misses.
Does the 1 ms figure apply to how long an IOMMU drain may take?

No. The 1 ms figure is the service deadline for unaffected devices. The activity calls for measuring IOMMU drains but states no numerical drain-time limit. The question is whether the restart and fault activity can occur while unaffected devices continue to meet their service deadlines.
If the trials report zero misses, can we immediately say the hypothesis is universally proved?

No. Zero misses in the planned 10,000 trials would be an observation within those trials, not a universal proof about every possible fault or operating condition. At this point even that observation is hypothetical: the node specifies the activity and measurements, not results.
And if a miss occurs, why does it matter even if most deadlines are met?

Because the hypothesis predicts zero unaffected-device 1 ms misses under the named DMA-flood and interrupt-storm conditions. A recorded miss would not match that zero-miss prediction for the condition observed. The activity does not state that a miss has occurred.
Should I describe the IOMMU drains as already successful because they are being measured?

No. Planning to measure IOMMU drains neither establishes that they complete as intended nor establishes their effect on deadline misses. The measurements are intended to help evaluate the drain-before-reuse hypothesis during restart.
Does FaultBench-1 tell us anything else about the setup?
Here, FaultBench-1 is the named setting for the 10,000 restart trials. No additional apparatus, configuration, or prior FaultBench-1 result is specified, so those details should remain unstated.
Can we say every restart trial will include rogue writes, stale DMA, and 100-kHz interrupts simultaneously?

Not from the activity as written. It calls for trials with those named conditions, but does not define their allocation or concurrency. We can preserve the full list without adding a trial-by-trial schedule.
What makes the unaffected-device measurement central rather than incidental?

The isolation goal requires unaffected devices to retain verified 1 ms service deadlines during driver faults and concurrent recovery. The deadline-miss measurement checks the timing outcome directly, while IOMMU-drain measurements address one proposed contributor to DMA containment. Both are needed to evaluate the stated hypothesis; neither is a result yet.
How would you state the activity in one careful sentence?

Run 10,000 FaultBench-1 driver-restart trials involving rogue writes, stale DMA, and 100-kHz interrupts, measuring IOMMU drains and unaffected-device 1 ms service-deadline misses to evaluate the zero-miss hypothesis, without presuming the outcome.
What did FaultBench-1 show in the restart trials?

Across 10,000 storm-driven restarts, FaultBench-1 showed zero cross-domain writes, zero post-reuse DMA writes, and zero unaffected-device 1 ms deadline misses. Those are the reported observations for these trials.
Are those three ways of saying the same thing?

No. Cross-domain writes concern writes crossing an isolation boundary. Post-reuse DMA writes concern DMA writes after reuse. Unaffected-device 1 ms deadline misses concern timely service for devices outside the fault. The evidence reports zero in each category.
Does zero cross-domain writes mean there were no memory writes at all?
No. It means no cross-domain writes were observed in the 10,000 storm-driven restarts. It does not say that drivers or devices performed no writes whatsoever.
What is the important qualifier in “post-reuse DMA writes”?

“Post-reuse” identifies the period relevant to that observation. The evidence reports no DMA writes after reuse; it does not say there was no DMA activity at any point during a restart. Keeping that qualifier matters when describing what FaultBench-1 showed.
And the timing result is specifically about unaffected devices?

Yes. FaultBench-1 recorded zero misses of unaffected devices’ 1 ms service deadlines across those 10,000 storm-driven restarts. The statement does not give a service-deadline result for the faulting driver.
Can I translate that into an average service time under 1 ms?
That would change the reported metric. The evidence is about deadline misses: none of the unaffected-device 1 ms deadlines were missed in those trials. It supplies no average service time.
Is this still a proposed experiment, or are we looking at results now?
This is a result: FaultBench-1 is reported to have shown those three zero counts over 10,000 storm-driven restarts. The counts should not be described merely as outcomes we hope to see.
How broadly can I phrase the zero-miss finding?

Keep it tied to the observed setting: 10,000 FaultBench-1 storm-driven restarts, with zero unaffected-device 1 ms deadline misses. The evidence does not establish a zero-miss result for every possible driver fault, device, or operating condition.
Does “storm-driven” specify an exact interrupt rate in this result?
The result itself says “storm-driven restarts” but does not state an interrupt rate. Its reported counts and trial total can be stated precisely without adding a rate to the evidence.
Does this tell us how long IOMMU draining took?
No drain duration is reported here. The DMA finding is specifically zero post-reuse DMA writes across the 10,000 storm-driven restarts; it is not a numerical measurement of drain time.
What about recovery duration or how much recovery work ran on the reserved cores?

Neither is quantified in this evidence. The stated timing observation is zero unaffected-device 1 ms deadline misses. That should not be converted into an unstated recovery time or a measurement of core use.
If I say the restarts caused no harm, is that precise enough?

It is too broad. The precise report is that FaultBench-1 observed zero cross-domain writes, zero post-reuse DMA writes, and zero unaffected-device 1 ms deadline misses in 10,000 storm-driven restarts. “No harm” could imply other outcomes that were not reported.
Can these observations be combined into a single pass count?

The evidence gives a total of 10,000 restarts and says the three specified event counts were zero across them. It does not define a separate pass criterion or provide additional per-trial classifications. Retaining the three named observations is clearer than replacing them with an undefined pass label.
Why report both the write results and the deadline result?

They cover different parts of the isolation concern. The write results describe observed containment at the cross-domain and post-reuse DMA boundaries. The deadline result describes observed service continuity for unaffected devices at the 1 ms threshold. Reporting only one side would omit part of what FaultBench-1 showed.
Would one missed 1 ms deadline still fit the reported result if the other 9,999 restarts had none?
No. The reported count is zero unaffected-device 1 ms deadline misses across the 10,000 storm-driven restarts. One observed miss would be a different result, even if the other restarts had none.
Likewise, is the DMA finding a low rate rather than an absolute zero in the trials?

It is reported as an absolute zero for post-reuse DMA writes in those trials, not as a low average rate. The boundary on the statement is the set of 10,000 observed storm-driven restarts, not a claim about all possible future executions.
How would you state the evidence without overstating it?

FaultBench-1 recorded 10,000 storm-driven restarts with no observed cross-domain writes, no post-reuse DMA writes, and no unaffected-device 1 ms deadline misses. That states the observed counts and their setting without turning them into an unrestricted guarantee.
What is the decision for the driver-isolation boundary?
Adopt per-driver domains, interrupt quotas, recovery-core isolation, and IOMMU drain-before-reuse. FaultBench-1 supports implementation of this approach, pending WCET certification.
What does “adopt” mean here? Are you saying the system has already been implemented and certified?

No. “Adopt” states the design decision: these are the controls selected for the implementation approach. FaultBench-1 provides support for implementing it, but WCET certification is still pending. The decision does not claim deployment or completed certification.
Can you unpack the four controls without adding a new design?

Per-driver domains separate drivers’ access boundaries. Interrupt quotas constrain the interrupt work attributable to a driver. Recovery-core isolation keeps recovery execution separate from cores reserved for real-time service. IOMMU drain-before-reuse makes draining outstanding DMA activity a condition of reuse. Those are the four elements named in the decision; it does not specify their detailed configuration.
Is a per-driver domain the same thing as an interrupt quota?

No. Per-driver domains concern access isolation, while interrupt quotas concern the demand imposed by interrupt activity. Both are adopted because containing memory effects and controlling an interrupt storm address different aspects of the driver boundary.
Does recovery-core isolation mean recovery cannot happen concurrently with service for unaffected devices?

No. The point is to separate recovery execution from reserved real-time cores so recovery can coexist with service for unaffected devices. Isolation of that work is part of the adopted approach; it is not a statement that recovery must wait until those devices are idle.
What exactly is being held back by “drain-before-reuse”?
